$comment: Misconception catalogue for Laws of Motion (pilot sample written in Phase 0 to fix the schema; to be completed and reviewed in Phase 3). 'implicates' lists skills whose weakness this misconception is evidence of; the detour planner intersects it with the prerequisite closure. Each tag owns one flashcard.

misconceptions.description: Assumes the normal force always equals mg, including on an incline or when other forces have perpendicular components.

flashcard.front: On a 30° incline, is the normal force on a resting block equal to its weight?
flashcard.back: No. The normal force balances only the component of weight perpendicular to the surface: N = mg cos θ (when nothing else pushes into the surface).

misconceptions.description: Uses mg sin θ for the perpendicular component and mg cos θ for the component along the incline.

flashcard.front: Which component of weight acts along a slope of angle θ?
flashcard.back: mg sin θ along the slope; mg cos θ perpendicular to it. The angle between the weight and the perpendicular to the slope equals θ.

misconceptions.description: Adds a 'force of motion' or 'force of the push' that has no agent after contact has ended.

flashcard.front: A box slides after you stop pushing. Is your push still a force on it?
flashcard.back: No. Every force needs an agent in contact (or a field). The box keeps moving because of inertia, and friction slows it.

misconceptions.description: Sets static friction equal to μs·N even when a smaller force would keep the body at rest.

flashcard.front: Is static friction always μs N?
flashcard.back: No. μs N is the maximum. Static friction is only as large as needed to prevent slipping, up to that maximum.

misconceptions.description: Points friction opposite the applied force rather than opposite the (tendency of) relative motion.

flashcard.back: Relative motion (or the tendency of relative motion) between the surfaces in contact, not necessarily the applied force.

misconceptions.description: Treats weight and normal force as a Newton's third law pair acting on the same body.

flashcard.front: Are weight and normal force on a book an action–reaction pair?
flashcard.back: No. Third-law pairs act on different bodies and are the same type of interaction. The pair of the book's weight is the book's pull on the Earth.

misconceptions.description: Answer has units of a different physical quantity (e.g. kg instead of N).

flashcard.back: Mass is in kg; weight is a force, W = mg, in newtons.
